summary: Describes NEC's Simple Middlebox Configuration protocol, version 3.0, for controlling middleboxes such as firewalls and network address translators. It implements the semantics from the Middlebox Communications framework in RFC 3989 and, unlike earlier experimental versions, uses binary messages. This is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4540 defines SIMCO, a protocol that lets an application talk directly to the firewall or address translator on its path. The application asks for a rule that permits one kind of traffic, and the device creates it, tells the application what it created, and removes it when the rule expires. The messages are small binary ones, because many of these devices are small and cheap.

questions: how to configure a firewall or nat remotely
subtitle: A compact binary protocol that lets applications ask firewalls and NATs to open pinholes and create address bindings.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and address translators can block a perfectly good packet stream, because the device does not know which port the application is about to use, and the application has no way to ask it.
tldr.mechanism: SIMCO defines a session between an application-side agent and a middlebox over TCP, in which the agent reserves, enables, inspects and deletes policy rules using small binary messages with a fixed 64-bit header and typed attributes.
tldr.outcome: Version 3.0 is a full implementation of the MIDCOM semantics in RFC 3989, with binary encoding instead of the ASCII of the earlier experimental versions, and it adds a policy disable rule transaction for use by intrusion detection systems. It is an Experimental specification.

today: RFC 4540 is an Experimental document published in May 2006. It was later updated by RFC 8996, which deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and updates the documents that refer to them.

sections.title: Why Middleboxes Need to Be Told
sections.content:
SIMCO is used to control firewalls and network address translators. As defined in RFC 3234, firewalls and NATs are classified as middleboxes: a device on the datagram path between source and destination that performs other functions than just IP routing. As outlined in RFC 3303, they are potential obstacles to packet streams, for example when dynamically negotiated UDP or TCP port numbers are used, as in many peer-to-peer communication applications.

SIMCO allows applications to communicate with the middleboxes on their datagram path in order to request a dynamic configuration at the middlebox that enables datagram streams to pass it. Applications can request pinholes at firewalls and address bindings at NATs. The semantics of the protocol are described in RFC 3989, and version 3.0 is a fully compliant implementation of those semantics, implementing all the message types and all the mandatory transactions, though not the optional group transactions.

Earlier experimental versions of SIMCO used simple ASCII encodings with augmented BNF for the syntax specification, which needs more resources for generation and parsing than binary encodings do. That matters for two reasons: for many applications, such as IP telephony, session setup times are critical, and some signalling protocols start retransmitting messages if setup is not completed within a certain time; and many middleboxes are rather small and relatively low-cost devices, for which support of resource-intensive protocols might be a problem. Version 3.0 therefore uses a simple and efficient binary encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall or a NAT can block a connection even when the application is behaving properly, because it does not know which port to expect. SIMCO lets the application tell the device directly which traffic to allow.

sections.title: Sessions and Transport
sections.content:
The protocol uses a session model with two parties: an agent representing one or more applications, and a middlebox. Both parties may participate in multiple sessions. An agent may simultaneously communicate with several middleboxes using one session per middlebox, and a middlebox may simultaneously communicate with several agents using one session per agent.

Sessions must run over a reliable transport layer protocol and are initiated by the agent. SIMCO implementations must support TCP, while other reliable transport protocols can be used as transport as well. When using TCP, middleboxes must wait for agents to connect on port 7626, which IANA has assigned to SIMCO servers. The session may be secured, if required, by either IPsec or TLS, to guarantee authentication, message integrity and confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: One conversation at a time between the application side and one device. The application opens it, and the device listens on a fixed port.

sections.title: The Header and the Payload
sections.content:
All SIMCO messages, from agent to middlebox and from middlebox to agent, are Type-Length-Value encoded using big endian, network ordered, binary data. Every message starts with the SIMCO header, which contains the message type, the message length and a message identifier, and the rest of the message, the payload, contains zero, one or more TLV message attributes.

The header has four fields and a size of 64 bits: the basic message type, the message sub-type, the message length excluding the SIMCO header in octets, and the transaction identifier. Only the combination of basic type and sub-type clearly identifies the type of a message. Each payload attribute starts with a 16-bit type field and a 16-bit length field, and the length field gives the length of the value field in octets. Eleven attribute types are defined, among them the SIMCO protocol version, the authentication challenge and token, the middlebox capabilities, the policy rule identifier, the group identifier, the policy rule lifetime and owner, the address tuple, and the PRR and PER parameter sets.

The transaction identifier is an arbitrary number identifying the transaction. In a request message the agent chooses an agent-unique value, so that the same agent never uses the same value in two different request messages belonging to the same session, and reply messages must contain the same value as the request they answer. In a notification message the middlebox chooses a middlebox-unique value in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a fixed eight-byte header naming what kind of message it is, how long it is, and which exchange it belongs to, followed by a list of typed values that carry the details.

sections.title: Session Control and Policy Rule Control
sections.content:
The message type in the header is divided into a basic type and a sub-type, and there are four basic types of message: request, positive reply, negative reply and notification. Messages sent from the agent to the middlebox are always of basic type request, while messages from the middlebox are one of the other three. The sub-type gives further information within the basic type, for example session establishment, session authentication, session termination, policy reserve rule, policy enable rule, policy disable rule, policy rule lifetime change, policy rule status and policy rule list.

The session control messages are the SE request, sent from the agent to ask the middlebox to establish a session, which carries the SIMCO version number and optionally a challenge asking the middlebox to authenticate itself; the SA request for session authentication; and the ST request for session termination. The middlebox sends a single reply per request and may also send unsolicited asynchronous session termination notifications.

The policy rule control messages are the PRR request, which reserves a rule, the PER request, which enables a rule, the PEA request, which enables a rule after a reservation, the PDR request, which disables a rule, the PLC request, which changes a rule's lifetime, the PRS request for the status of a rule and the PRL request for a list of rules. SIMCO adds one transaction to those defined in RFC 3989, the policy disable rule, which is used by security functions such as intrusion detection and attack detection, lets the agent block a specified kind of traffic, and has priority above policy enable rules: when it is established, all conflicting enable rules, including ones that only partially overlap, are terminated, and no new conflicting enable rule can be established before it is terminated. Support for this transaction is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three messages for the conversation itself, open, authenticate and close, and a set for the rules: reserve one, switch it on, change its lifetime, ask for its status, or delete it.

sections.title: The Session State Machine
sections.content:
For each session there is a session state machine. Request transactions are written as a descriptor of the request message, a slash and a descriptor of the reply, so a successful session establishment is SE/SE, and notification transactions are written as the notification descriptor alone, for example AST. Initially all sessions are in state CLOSED. A successful SE transaction can change the state either to NOAUTH or to OPEN; from NOAUTH a successful SA transaction changes the state to OPEN, and a failed SA transaction changes it back to CLOSED. Successful ST transactions and AST notifications move a session from NOAUTH or from OPEN to CLOSED.

A SIMCO session is established in state OPEN, which is the only state in which the middlebox accepts requests other than SE, SA and ST. The SE request is only applicable when the session is in state CLOSED; if it arrives in NOAUTH or OPEN the middlebox answers with a negative reply of type request not applicable and leaves the state unchanged. A middlebox may also refuse the SE request because it lacks resources, because the selected network connection and its protocol specific parameters are not acceptable, or because the security properties of the connection do not meet its requirements, and in each of those cases it returns a negative reply and closes the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: A session starts closed, opens after the handshake, and closes when either side ends it or the connection drops. Rules can only be asked for once the session is fully open.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo notes that middleboxes are usually operated for improving network security and for extending the IP address space, and that configuring them from an external entity looks quite counterproductive on the first glimpse, since an attacker using this could configure the middlebox so that no filtering is applied any more, or so that NAT bindings are configured for malicious use. Four threats are listed. A man-in-the-middle attack intercepts the messages exchanged between the agent and the middlebox and changes their content on the fly, so that from the agent's view the middlebox is configured properly while it is not, and the attacker can open pinholes that compromise the protected network's security. Changing content means the requested rule is not the one configured, but some other unwanted configuration is, which lets an attacker open the firewall for its own traffic. Replaying already sent messages configures the middlebox so that hosts can set up policy rules without the permission of an application-level gateway or system administrator. Wiretapping covers an already configured policy rule being reused by other hosts when it was configured with too broad a wildcarding.

SIMCO can rely on IPsec mechanisms to ensure proper operation. When it does, it uses IPsec in transport mode with an authentication header and an encapsulating security payload, so that the traffic between agent and middlebox is protected: the authentication header protects the whole packet against content changes and replaying, and the ESP header prevents wiretapping. At either the agent or middlebox side, the IP addresses, the TCP transport and the port numbers should be pre-configured where possible, and only packets from the pre-configured address should be accepted. The authentication keys are pre-configured at each side, and for replay protection the use of a key management system is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is blunt about the risk: giving an outside program the power to change a firewall is exactly what an attacker would like, so the traffic between the two must be protected. It recommends IPsec, with the authentication header stopping changes and replays and the encrypted part stopping anyone reading the traffic.

fields.name: Basic Type
fields.desc: Request, positive reply, negative reply or notification.

fields.name: Sub-Type
fields.desc: Identifies the message within the basic type.

fields.name: Message Length
fields.desc: Length of the message excluding the header, in octets.

fields.name: Transaction Identifier
fields.desc: Identifies the transaction; the reply carries the same value as the request.

items.label: REQUEST
items.desc: A basic message type, always used from agent to middlebox.

items.label: POSITIVE REPLY
items.desc: A basic message type, sent by the middlebox.

items.label: NEGATIVE REPLY
items.desc: A basic message type, sent by the middlebox.

items.label: NOTIFICATION
items.desc: A basic message type, sent by the middlebox.

items.label: PRD
items.desc: Policy rule deletion, positive reply only.

items.label: PES
items.desc: Policy enable rule status, positive reply only.

items.label: PDS
items.desc: Policy disable rule status, positive reply only.

items.label: BFM
items.desc: Badly formed message received, a notification.

items.label: ARE
items.desc: Asynchronous policy rule event, a notification.
